title: The AI industry has already spent $65 million ahead of the midterm elections with no signs of slowing down.
excerpt: The AI industry is showing no signs of slowing down as it seeks to use the midterm elections to shape future regulations.
content_html:
Some of the biggest names in AI and tech are using the midterm elections to fight a proxy war over the future of their industry.

Anthropic, Meta, and OpenAI President Greg Brockman are among those linked to networks of outside groups and super PACs aimed at shaping the next Congress and the balance of power in some state legislatures.

Already, the groups have spent over $65 million, with tens of millions still left in reserve. The full total may not be known for some time due to so-called "dark money" groups that don't have to regularly disclose their expenditures.

The Trump administration has generally taken a friendly approach to AI regulation, but tensions have flared after the White House slowed the release of the latest frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Both companies are also closely watching what, if anything, the Trump administration and lawmakers decide to do about China-based open weight AI models like Moonshot AI's popular Kimi K3.

AI is facing a critical moment as more people are using more advanced models than ever before. At the same time, the industry has become deeply unpopular. Some states are even considering enacting data center moratoriums like the one New York Gov. Kathy Hochul recently signed into law.

Here are the super PACs to keep an eye on as the year progresses.

Leading the Future

The biggest player so far is Leading the Future, a pro-AI network of super PACs associated with some of Silicon Valley's tech elite.

The group's main super PAC has raised just under $76 million as of the end of June, according to FEC filings.

That included:

  • $50 million from Andreesen Horowitz;
  • $25 million from OpenAI CEO Greg Brockman and his wife Anna;
  • $25 million from Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz ($12.5 million each)
  • $100,000 from Perplexity.

Brockman explained his philosophy on political giving in a lengthy post on X at the end of 2025, writing in part that "being pro-AI does not mean being anti-regulation."

OpenAI has distanced itself from Brockman's donations after Leading the Future received significant attention, saying he is acting in his personal capacity.

The network includes a super PAC for Democratic races, Think Big, along with a GOP-focused super PAC, American Mission.

Leading the Future has redirected $20 million to Think Big. FEC filings show that SV Angel Founder Ron Conway kicked in another $500,000 to the Democratic-focused super PAC.

Meanwhile, 8VC Founder Joe Lonsdale gave $250,000 to American Mission. Leading the Future has also redirected another $20 million to the Republican-focused super PAC.

The group said in an August 2025 release that it plans to serve as the "political and policy center of gravity for the AI industry" and will "support candidates aligned with the pro-AI agenda" and "oppose those that do not."

Think Big and American Mission have spent over $29 million so far. Leading the Future is also sitting on more than $31 million, leaving the group plenty in its coffers as the midterms approach.

So far, Think Big has spent over $18 million so far, over $7.6 million more than American Mission, its Republican focused counterpart.

Of the $18 million, $8 million was spent against Assemblyman Alex Bores in the Democratic primary for New York's 12th congressional district. Bores, who once worked at Palantir, called for stronger regulations of AI, which he had pursued during his time in the New York legislature. He ultimately finished second to fellow Assemblyman Micah Lasher, who also supported stronger AI regulations. Think Big also spent another roughly $7.2 million backing a handful of Democratic US House hopefuls, the most of which ($1.4 million) was on former Congressman Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr.'s unsuccessful comeback bid in Illinois.

American Mission has spent $10.7 million thus far. In total, the group has tried to boost 19 GOP candidates running for Congress. The group spent over $960,000 boosting Georgia Republican Jim Kingston, the son of former US Congressman Jack Kingston.

Leading the Future also has an allied nonprofit called Build American AI, which is not required to disclose its donors.

Public First

In response to Leading the Future, two former congressmen — Republican Chris Stewart of Utah and Democrat Brad Carson of Oklahoma — have formed a competing political network, Public First, to back candidates who support AI regulation.

Public First Action, the umbrella organization for a trio of super PACs, is not required to disclose its donors. In June, the group said it had raised $80 million thus far. Anthropic has donated $40 million to the group.

Carson previously told Business Insider that he felt good about Public First's odds, even if the group was likely to be outspent by Leading The Future. At the time, Public First Action aimed to raise $50 million.

"We have $50 million and 85% of public sentiment. They have 15% of public settlement, and $100 million," Carson said. "I will take our side of that bet any day."

Anthropic said it doubled its support, the AI startup had first donated $20 million in February, due to the rapid advancements in AI, including the development of its Claude Mythos model. Mythos is so advanced that, as of late July, it remains only accessible to a limited number of companies and organizations due to concerns about its hacking capabilities.

"Our donation to Public First Action is one way in which we're trying to raise the salience of this urgent policy debate," Anthropic said in its July donation announcement.

Anthropic has said its donations "cannot be used to influence the election of any candidate for federal, state, or local office," but Public First Action's allied super PACs engage in exactly those types of activities.

The group has two super PACs: one that supports candidates from both parties called Public First; one that supports Democrats, called Jobs and Democracy PAC, and another that supports Republicans, called Defending Our Values PAC.

Public First is the smallest of three super PACs, though it has attracted the support of the biggest name. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei donated $1 million to the group. Other Anthropic staffers have donated an additional $2.1 million.

Public First Action and Public First have donated over $19 million combined. The next largest donor is Jan Leike, who leads the Alignment Science team at Anthropic. Leike donated $100,000 and separately donated an additionall $400,000 to Public First.

Jobs and Democracy PAC has spent just under $20 million so far. The overwhelming majority of those funds, just over $15 million, was spent on boosting Bores during his unsuccessful primary campaign. The group has spent another $1.6 million on boosting Rep. Valerie Foushee of North Carolina, who survived a closely-watched Democratic primary.

Defending Our Values PAC has spent $5 million thus far. Like Jobs and Democracy, its largest supporters are also Public First Action and Public First, which combined have sent over $5.2 million to the group

Of those funds spent thus far, Republican Carlos De La Cruz has been the biggest beneficiary, with over $1.4 million spent thus far on pushing his election in a closely-watched US House race for a redrawn district in Texas. The group has spent another roughly $1 million to boost Rep. Celeste Maloy of Utah, who, due to redistricting, is running for reelection in a reconfigured district.

Two Meta-backed groups

Meta is also getting into the spending game, establishing two different groups to support candidates aligned with their vision for AI regulation.

Unlike the other groups, Meta's efforts will focus primarily on the state level.

One group, called Mobilizing Economic Transformation Across (Meta) California, focuses specifically on the Golden State, where Meta is headquartered.

"As home to many of the world's leading AI companies, California's innovation economy has an outsized impact on America's economic growth, job creation, and global competitiveness," a Meta spokesperson previously told Business Insider. "But Sacramento's regulatory environment could stifle innovation, block AI progress, and put California's technology leadership at risk."

The spokesperson added that the PAC would back candidates in both parties who "recognize California's vital role in AI development and embrace policies that will keep the state at the forefront of the global tech ecosystem."

Meta gave $20 million to its California-focused PAC in August 2025, according to documents recently filed with the California Secretary of State.

The California-focused group has spent over $4.3 million thus far. The largest beneficiary has been Scott Sakakihara, a Democrat running for a state Senate seat that covers part of Silicon Valley. The group has spent $1.3 million boosting Sakakihara's run.

A separate group, the American Technology Excellence Project, is focused on races in other states.

"Amid a growing patchwork of inconsistent regulations that threaten homegrown innovation and investments in AI, state lawmakers are uniquely positioned to ensure that America remains a global technology leader," Meta VP of Public Policy Brian Rice said in a statement to Business Insider.

The group is a 527, a special kind of nonprofit specifically created to influence elections. Unlike so-called "dark money" groups, 527s have to reveal their donors.

Meta donated $45 million to the group, according to information filed with the IRS.

Of those funds, Meta has redirected $5.5 million to a pair of allied super PACs that will operate at the state level. The super PAC supporting Republicans is called Forge the Future, and the group supporting Democrats is called Making Our Tomorrow.

An Illinois-based branch of Making Our Tomorrow has reported spending over $650,000 thus far. While a Texas-based branch of Forge Our Future has spent over $1.3 million thus far.

blocks.html_en: So far, Think Big has spent over $18 million so far, over $7.6 million more than American Mission, its Republican focused counterpart.

blocks.html_en: Of the $18 million, $8 million was spent against Assemblyman Alex Bores in the Democratic primary for New York's 12th congressional district. He ultimately finished second to fellow Assemblyman Micah Lasher, who also supported stronger AI regulations. Think Big also spent another roughly $7.2 million backing a handful of Democratic US House hopefuls, the most of which ($1.4 million) was on former Congressman Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr.'s unsuccessful comeback bid in Illinois.

blocks.html_en: Brent Griffiths is a senior reporter at Business Insider who covers AI and tech.Previously, he worked at the Washington Post as a researcher on Power Up and the Finance 202. He started his career at Politico where he worked on the web production team and covered breaking news. His passion for covering politics has only grown since he cut his teeth covering the presidential campaign as a student journalist. He's also contributed to the Almanac of American Politics.

sentences.en: OpenAI
sentences.zh: 开放人工智能

content_html_zh:
人工智能和科技领域的一些知名人士正在利用中期选举来就其行业的未来展开代理人战争。

Anthropic、Meta 和 OpenAI 总裁格雷格·布罗克曼 (Greg Brockman) 都与外部团体和超级政治行动委员会网络有联系，旨在塑造下一届国会和一些州立法机构的权力平衡。

这些团体已经花费了超过 6500 万美元，还有数千万美元作为储备。 由于所谓的“黑钱”团体不必定期披露其支出，因此在一段时间内可能无法得知全部费用。

特朗普政府总体上对人工智能监管采取了友好的态度，但在白宫放慢了 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 最新前沿模型的发布之后，紧张局势加剧。 两家公司还在密切关注特朗普政府和立法者决定如何处理基于中国的开放权重人工智能模型，例如 Moonshot AI 广受欢迎的 Kimi K3。

随着越来越多的人使用比以往更先进的模型，人工智能正面临关键时刻。 与此同时，这个行业已经变得非常不受欢迎。 一些州甚至正在考虑暂停数据中心，例如纽约州州长。 凯西·霍赫尔 (Kathy Hochul) 最近签署成为法律。

以下是今年值得关注的超级政治行动委员会。

引领未来

迄今为止最大的参与者是Leading the Future，这是一个由超级政治行动委员会组成的支持人工智能的网络，与硅谷的一些科技精英有联系。

根据 FEC 文件，截至 6 月底，该集团主要的超级 PAC 已筹集近 7600 万美元。

其中包括：

  • Andreesen Horowitz 投资 5000 万美元；
  • OpenAI 首席执行官格雷格·布罗克曼 (Greg Brockman) 和他的妻子安娜 (Anna) 提供 2500 万美元；
  • 马克·安德森 (Marc Andreessen) 和本·霍洛维茨 (Ben Horowitz) 出资 2500 万美元（各 1250 万美元）
  • 来自困惑的 100,000 美元。

布罗克曼在 2025 年底在 X 上发表了一篇长篇文章，解释了他的政治捐赠理念，部分写道“支持人工智能并不意味着反对监管”。

在“引领未来”受到广泛关注后，OpenAI 与布罗克曼的捐赠保持了距离，称他是以个人身份行事。

该网络包括一个负责民主党竞选的超级政治行动委员会“Think Big”，以及一个专注于共和党的超级政治行动委员会“美国使命”。

“Leading Future”已将 2000 万美元重新定向到“Think Big”。 FEC 文件显示，SV Angel 创始人罗恩·康威 (Ron Conway) 又向以民主党为重点的超级政治行动委员会捐款 50 万美元。

与此同时，8VC 创始人 Joe Lonsdale 向 American Mission 捐赠了 25 万美元。 “引领未来”还向以共和党为中心的超级政治行动委员会重新定向了另外 2000 万美元。

该组织在 2025 年 8 月的一份新闻稿中表示，计划成为“人工智能行业的政治和政策重心”，并将“支持符合支持人工智能议程的候选人”并“反对那些不支持人工智能的候选人”。

Think Big 和 American Mission 迄今为止已花费超过 2900 万美元。 Leading the Future 还拥有超过 3100 万美元的资金，随着中期选举的临近，该集团的金库里还有充足的资金。

到目前为止，Think Big 已花费超过 1800 万美元，比专注于共和党的同行 American Mission 多出 760 万美元。

在 1800 万美元中，有 800 万美元用于在纽约第 12 国会选区的民主党初选中对抗众议员亚历克斯·博雷斯 (Alex Bores)。 曾在 Palantir 工作过的 Bores 呼吁加强对人工智能的监管，这是他在纽约立法机构任职期间所追求的。 他最终排名第二，落后于同样支持加强人工智能监管的议员米卡·拉舍尔 (Micah Lasher)。 Think Big 还花费了大约 720 万美元支持少数民主党美国众议院候选人，其中大部分（140 万美元）投给了前国会议员众议员。 小杰西·杰克逊在伊利诺伊州的复出未果。

美国宣教团迄今已花费 1070 万美元。 该组织总共试图推动 19 名共和党候选人竞选国会议员。 该组织花费超过 96 万美元支持佐治亚州共和党人吉姆·金斯顿 (Jim Kingston)，他是前美国国会议员杰克·金斯顿 (Jack Kingston) 的儿子。

“引领未来”还有一个名为“Build American AI”的联盟非营利组织，该组织无需披露其捐助者。

公众第一

为了回应“引领未来”，两位前国会议员——犹他州的共和党人克里斯·斯图尔特(Chris Stewart)和俄克拉荷马州的民主党人布拉德·卡森(Brad Carson)——组建了一个相互竞争的政治网络“公共优先”，以支持支持人工智能监管的候选人。

公共优先行动是由三个超级政治行动委员会组成的伞式组织，无需披露其捐助者。 6 月，该集团表示迄今为止已筹集 8000 万美元。 Anthropic 已向该组织捐赠了 4000 万美元。

卡森此前告诉《商业内幕》，他对“公共优先”的胜算感到满意，即使该组织的支出可能超过“引领未来”。 当时，Public First Action 的目标是筹集 5000 万美元。

“我们有 5000 万美元和 85% 的公众情绪。 他们拥有 15% 的公共结算权和 1 亿美元，”卡森说。 “我随时都会站在我们这边。”

Anthropic 表示，由于人工智能的快速进步，包括其 Claude Mythos 模型的开发，其支持力度增加了一倍，这家人工智能初创公司在 2 月份首次捐赠了 2000 万美元。 Mythos 是如此先进，以至于截至 7 月下旬，由于对其黑客能力的担忧，它仍然只有少数公司和组织可以访问。

Anthropic 在 7 月份的捐赠公告中表示：“我们对公共优先行动组织的捐款是我们试图提高这一紧急政策辩论的重要性的一种方式。”

Anthropic 表示，其捐款“不能用于影响联邦、州或地方办公室任何候选人的选举”，但“公共第一行动”的联盟超级政治行动委员会正是从事此类活动。

该组织有两个超级政治行动委员会：一个支持两党候选人，称为“公众优先”；另一个是支持两党候选人的政治行动委员会。一个支持民主党，称为“就业与民主”政治行动委员会，另一个支持共和党，称为“捍卫我们的价值观”政治行动委员会。

Public First 是三个超级政治行动委员会中最小的一个，尽管它吸引了最知名人士的支持。 Anthropic 首席执行官 Dario Amodei 向该组织捐赠了 100 万美元。 Anthropic 的其他员工还额外捐赠了 210 万美元。

Public First Action 和 Public First 的捐赠总额已超过 1900 万美元。 第二大捐赠者是 Jan Leike，他领导着 Anthropic 的对齐科学团队。 雷克捐赠了 10 万美元，并另外向 Public First 捐赠了 40 万美元。

到目前为止，就业与民主 PAC 已花费近 2000 万美元。 这些资金中的绝大多数（刚刚超过 1500 万美元）都用于支持博雷斯在初选活动中的失败。 该组织又花费了 160 万美元来提升众议员的实力。 北卡罗来纳州的瓦莱丽·富希 (Valerie Foushee) 在备受关注的民主党初选中幸存下来。

捍卫我们的价值观 PAC 迄今已花费 500 万美元。 与就业和民主组织一样，其最大的支持者也是 Public First Action 和 Public First，这两家组织总共向该组织捐赠了超过 520 万美元

在迄今为止花费的资金中，共和党人卡洛斯·德拉克鲁兹是最大的受益者，迄今为止，他已经花费了超过 140 万美元来推动他在备受关注的美国众议院竞选中赢得德克萨斯州重新划定的选区。 该组织又花费了大约 100 万美元来提升众议员的实力。 犹他州的塞莱斯特·马洛伊 (Celeste Maloy) 由于选区重新划分，正在重新配置的选区竞选连任。

两个元支持的团体

Meta 也参与了支出游戏，建立了两个不同的团体来支持符合人工智能监管愿景的候选人。

与其他组织不同，Meta 的努力将主要集中在州一级。

一个名为“动员整个加利福尼亚州 (Meta) 经济转型”的组织专门关注 Meta 总部所在的金州。

Meta 发言人此前告诉《商业内幕》：“作为许多世界领先的人工智能公司的所在地，加州的创新经济对美国的经济增长、创造就业机会和全球竞争力有着巨大的影响。” “但萨克拉门托的监管环境可能会扼杀创新，阻碍人工智能的进步，并使加州的技术领先地位面临风险。”

该发言人补充说，PAC 将支持两党候选人，他们“认识到加州在人工智能发展中的重要作用，并采取政策，使该州保持在全球科技生态系统的最前沿。”

根据最近向加州国务卿提交的文件，Meta 于 2025 年 8 月向专注于加州的 PAC 捐赠了 2000 万美元。

迄今为止，这个专注于加州的组织已花费超过 430 万美元。 最大的受益者是民主党人斯科特·坂原（Scott Sakakihara），他正在竞选覆盖硅谷部分地区的州参议院席位。 该组织已花费 130 万美元来推动 Sakakihara 的发展。

一个单独的组织，即美国技术卓越项目，专注于其他州的比赛。

公共政策元副总裁布莱恩·赖斯（Brian Rice）在给《商业内幕》的一份声明中表示：“越来越多的不一致的法规威胁着本土创新和人工智能投资，州立法者处于独特的地位，可以确保美国保持全球技术领先地位。”

该组织是 527 组织，是一种专门为影响选举而创建的特殊非营利组织。 与所谓的“黑钱”团体不同，527 必须公开其捐助者。

根据美国国税局 (IRS) 提交的信息，Meta 向该组织捐赠了 4500 万美元。

在这些资金中，Meta 已将 550 万美元转入两个将在州一级运作的联盟超级政治行动委员会。 支持共和党的超级政治行动委员会被称为“打造未来”，支持民主党的组织被称为“创造我们的明天”。

“创造我们的明天”位于伊利诺伊州的分支机构报告称，迄今为止已支出超过 65 万美元。 Forge Our Future 位于德克萨斯州的分支机构迄今为止已花费超过 130 万美元。

布伦特·格里菲斯 (Brent Griffiths) 是《商业内幕》(Business Insider) 的高级记者，报道人工智能和科技。此前，他曾在《华盛顿邮报》担任 Power Up 和 Finance 202 的研究员。 他的职业生涯始于 Politico，在网络制作团队工作并报道突发新闻。 自从他作为一名学生记者开始报道总统竞选以来，他对报道政治的热情与日俱增。 他还为《美国政治年鉴》做出了贡献。
